title: Independent audit desk for city surveillance vendors
one_liner: A fixed-price monthly service that checks whether a city's license-plate-reader and drone vendor is actually following the city's own sharing rules, and hands the council a report it can cite.
customer: City auditors, city attorneys and city managers (plus police oversight boards) in the roughly 50+ cities that cancelled or suspended Flock and the many more that kept ALPR or drone programs under new council conditions. Buyers pay $1.2k-2.5k/month per city from the auditor, city attorney or IT budget, well under the informal-procurement threshold.
problem: Cities cannot verify what the surveillance vendor does with their data. Mountain View's own audit found a statewide-lookup setting active on 29 of 30 cameras since program start, with 250+ outside agencies running about 600,000 searches in 12 months, and the vendor kept no records that would show what was shared. Oxnard's vendor silently re-enabled a nationwide query feature. Evanston found cameras reinstalled after cancellation. Dayton found 7,100+ searches for immigration enforcement that city policy prohibited. Councils now write audit duties into ordinances, but the auditor's office has no tooling.
solution: A vendor-neutral audit service (Flock, Axon, Motorola/Vigilant, drone platforms). The city exports the search and audit logs and sharing-settings screenshots it can already download. The service ingests them and runs a rules engine against the city's adopted policy: searches with no case number or with vague reason codes, out-of-state or federal agencies, immigration-related terms, off-hours spikes, and diffs of the network-sharing settings month to month to catch silent config changes. Output is a council-ready quarterly report and a same-week alert on config drift. Add-on: a field check that cameras a council ordered off are really off, since Evanston found them reinstalled.
why_now: 53 cities across 20 states had cancelled or rejected Flock by mid-2026 over unauthorized federal access. New state laws (Colorado SB 26-070 warrant rule, Washington SB 6002, Kentucky HB 58 90-day retention cap, Maine's ALPR law) add compliance duties. Atlanta's ordinance, held in committee and taken up again in September 2026, would require monthly internal access audits and annual independent technical audits managed by the City Auditor. Drone-as-first-responder approvals (Stockton, Federal Way, Santa Fe, Whittier) are expanding the audit surface.
revenue_model: $4.5k one-time baseline configuration and log audit, then $1.2k-2.5k/month monitoring and quarterly council report. Upsell: annual independent technical audit that ordinances like Atlanta's require, priced $15k-40k for larger cities. Multi-year contracts through city auditor offices.
non_obvious_insight: The market is created by oversight ordinances, not by the surveillance vendors. Every ordinance that says 'audit monthly' is an unfunded mandate on a three-person auditor's office, and the failure mode is configuration drift, not sophisticated data science. Evidence: Mountain View's statewide lookup ran from launch until Jan 5, 2026 unnoticed (https://www.mv-voice.com/police/2026/01/30/amid-immigration-crackdown-mountain-view-discovers-unauthorized-access-to-license-plate-data/). The audit findings and 53-city cancellation count are in https://www.techtimes.com/articles/319317/20260629/flock-safety-crosses-100000-cameras-53-cities-cancel-over-unauthorized-federal-data-access.htm. Atlanta's proposed monthly internal and annual independent audits are at https://www.atlantanewsfirst.com/2026/09/22/atlanta-weighs-sweeping-rules-monthly-audits-surveillance-tech/. New Hanover County's commissioners called for 'explicit guardrails' before restoring cameras: https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9840468/north-carolina/new-hanover-county/commissioners-cite-privacy-shifting-vendor-policies-and-misuse-when-cancelling-flock-alpr-contract. Cities that keep the cameras need proof of compliance to survive the next council vote, and the audit report is that proof.
first_30_days: File public-records requests in about 25 cities that cancelled or kept ALPR for the audit-log export format and sharing-settings history, and build a parser for it. Produce one free 'configuration drift' teardown for a friendly city attorney or a councilmember who championed the cancellation. Pitch the $4.5k baseline audit to auditors and attorneys in cities with surveillance-oversight ordinances (Seattle, San Diego, Oakland, Cambridge, Urbana) and to those now drafting them (Atlanta). Sign 3 pilots. Main risk: vendor cooperation and export formats, so start with cities that already run their own audits.

title: Licensing Workbench for Smallsat Operators
one_liner: A structured software system of record for satellite licensing across spectrum, debris, remote sensing and export control.
customer: Smallsat startups, university missions and new sovereign programs that currently pay law firms and consultants $50-300k per licensing cycle.
problem: Launches and deployments are at record levels (4,517 satellites in 2025), and licensing throughput is the hidden bottleneck. Operators juggle FCC, ITU, NOAA remote-sensing, debris-mitigation and export-control filings. Rules are changing (reported FCC rewrite, the 5-year deorbit rule, the proposed EU Space Act).
solution: A workbench with deterministic calculators (debris assessment, collision probability), templated filings, an ITU coordination tracker, deadline management and an insurer-ready data pack. Add a marketplace to hire specialist counsel. It is not a thin AI wrapper: the value is the structured filing data model and up-to-date rules.
why_now: The 2025-26 regulatory changes and a growing flood of new operators. The EU Space Act, FCC modernization and stricter debris rules all raise the compliance load.
revenue_model: $1-3k per month per mission. Per-filing fees. Referral fees from counsel and consultants.
non_obvious_insight: Every launch boom makes regulatory throughput the binding constraint. The company that owns the data model of a filing becomes the system of record.
first_30_days: Interview 15 smallsat licensing leads about their last filing. Build one calculator plus a deadline tracker for a specific filing, for example an FCC debris assessment. Sign five paying pilots at $500-1,000 per month.

title: Micro-Bounties for Humans to Rescue Stuck Robots
one_liner: An on-demand app where robots and AVs post 30-second physical tasks (close a door, plug in a charger, move a cone, lift a robot over a curb) and nearby humans get paid instantly.
customer: Operators of sidewalk delivery robots, robotaxi and AV fleets, drone hubs, cleaning robots and warehouse AMRs, paying about $3-15 per task.
problem: Autonomy fails at the last physical one percent. Only 54% of Waymo's first 86M miles carried a passenger and each reset cycle takes about 2 hours. Dispatching a staffer or tow costs far more than the fix, and each fleet builds its own field-ops team.
solution: An SDK in which the robot emits a help request with location, photos and a vision-language-model task description. Nearby vetted people accept it, the robot's own sensors verify completion, and payout is instant. Strict safety rules prevent anyone touching moving machines. Start with door-ajar, debris and stuck-at-curb tasks.
why_now: Robot fleets are scaling faster than field crews (Waymo about 500k rides a week, sidewalk fleets in the thousands), and AV firms have reportedly begun paying gig workers for simple physical fixes. Vision-language models can now write the task description automatically.
revenue_model: 20-30% take on each task plus a monthly platform fee per fleet.
non_obvious_insight: Every robot fleet needs a thin, geographically spread hands-and-feet layer that scales with robot count. A two-sided micro-labor network is cheaper than dedicated field teams, and because the robot is the buyer, demand is programmable and grows with every deployment.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with a delivery-robot or campus-robot operator, recruit 50 local gig workers, and dispatch manually by SMS. Sign a $2k a month pilot with a small fleet, run 500 tasks, and publish resolution-time data.

title: Crawlspace Robots for the 44-Year-Old House
one_liner: Small tracked robots that scan, photograph and eventually air-seal and insulate the crawlspaces and attics humans dread, starting as a quote-enabling survey service.
customer: Home inspectors, insurers and home-warranty firms (moisture and water-damage claims), and HVAC, insulation and foundation-repair contractors who need access before quoting. Later: weatherization programs.
problem: Median home age is 44 years, 62% of homeowners now choose repair over replace, and 78% of those with unstarted projects have no quotes. Contractors avoid the crawlspace visit because it is slow, dirty and unsafe, so inspectors skip it and quotes are guesses. It is the most avoided labor in the house.
solution: Phase 1: a low-cost tracked robot with camera, thermal and LiDAR plus a vision-language pipeline producing a 10-minute survey covering moisture, insulation, duct leaks, pest and mold signs and structural issues, sold as an add-on to inspectors and a pre-quote survey to contractors. Phase 2: tool attachments for air sealing and topping insulation. Phase 3: crawlspace-as-a-service retrofit fleet.
why_now: Cheap edge compute, reliable vision-language defect classification and low-cost thermal sensors. Labor shortages make anyone willing to crawl scarce. Insurers want moisture data and aging stock keeps growing.
revenue_model: $149-249 per survey (inspector add-on or contractor pre-quote), insurer report fees, later per-job retrofit revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The robot does not need to replace skilled trades, only the worst 20 minutes of their job. Access is the friction, and a proprietary library of real crawlspace conditions is the moat.
first_30_days: Build v0 from a hobby tracked chassis, action camera and thermal sensor (about $3K). Run 30 free surveys for 5 home inspectors and 2 insulation contractors. Track how often findings convert to jobs and test pricing.

title: Compute Boilers: Servers That Heat Buildings
one_liner: Install liquid-cooled inference servers in the boiler rooms of hotels, dorms, pools and laundries, sell the compute, and give the building cheap hot water.
customer: Hotels, university housing, municipal pools and YMCAs, multifamily buildings with central hot water, and laundries. They get cheaper heat. Inference providers buy the compute.
problem: Large AI sites wait years in interconnection queues, yet buildings already have continuous thermal loads, existing 3-phase service and unused headroom. Sub-MW loads avoid large-load studies. Owners face pressure to electrify hot water and building-emissions fines such as NYC's Local Law 97.
solution: Sealed 30-100 kW direct-to-chip liquid-cooled modules plumbed into building hot-water loops that capture most of the heat. The company owns and operates the hardware and sells GPU-hours to inference customers through a neocloud partner. The host gets heat at a discount to its gas or electric cost. First product: 20-40 kW pilots at about 10 hotels and pools in one metro.
why_now: Direct-to-chip liquid cooling is now standard, AI demand exceeds grid supply, small-model inference fits ordinary fiber, and UK pool and hot-water-cylinder server projects prove the model.
revenue_model: Compute revenue share, heat sold to hosts at 50-70% of their current fuel cost, and GPU-lender financing of the hardware.
non_obvious_insight: The grid is not short of electrons. It is short of interconnection at big sites. Sub-MW building sites already have service and a thermal sink, and heat reuse lowers hosting cost below any standalone data center, so the queue is bypassed.
first_30_days: Sign LOIs with five hospitality or pool operators in a state with cheap power and good fiber. Run heat-load audits. Spec a module with a liquid-cooling OEM. Get a GPU-lender term sheet. Deploy a 10 kW test unit at one site.

title: Credit Union Tokenized Deposit Network
one_liner: Give thousands of small credit unions a shared 24/7 tokenized-deposit settlement network so they can answer the 'war for deposits' together instead of losing it one by one.
customer: Credit unions ($500M-$10B assets), state leagues and CUSOs, and later their members and local merchants.
problem: Banks describe the stablecoin fight as a '$6 trillion war for deposits' (CoinDesk, 2026-09-14). No single credit union has the scale to run its own token or build 24/7 settlement, and Zelle-style networks are controlled by big banks. Members get weekday-hours payments between institutions.
solution: A CUSO-owned network of tokenized member deposits (not a stablecoin at first), starting with 24/7 credit-union-to-credit-union settlement for shared branching and member P2P, then bill pay and merchant acceptance. A licensed trust-bank or custody partner handles the token layer and reserves.
why_now: The OCC charter wave (Circle 2026-07-10, Coinbase April, Bridge and Crypto.com conditional) has made compliant token infrastructure available to partner with. Citi and Coinbase launched corporate stablecoin acceptance on 2026-09-28, and the GENIUS Act takes effect around Jan 2027 (verify).
revenue_model: Network transaction fees, SaaS to member credit unions, and a share of reserve income on the settlement layer.
non_obvious_insight: The cooperative structure is the unfair advantage. Credit unions already share ATMs, branching and core processing through CUSOs, so a shared money layer is a natural extension that gives 4,500 small institutions scale none could build alone.
first_30_days: Get LOIs from five credit unions through one state league. Run a paper pilot for inter-credit-union treasury settlement with a partner trust bank, and charge pilot fees for design work and integration.

title: Search-Fund Accelerator for Buying Scrap Yards
one_liner: A cohort program that turns laid-off mid-career managers into owner-operators of small scrap yards, e-scrap shops and transfer stations. It brings deal sourcing, environmental diligence and SBA-lender access.
customer: Laid-off ops, finance and product managers with severance or savings of about $100-300K, who pay cohort tuition and a success fee. Second customer: retiring owners of scrap and recycling businesses who want a successor buyer. SBA lenders are a channel.
problem: Mid-career job searches now run 7-13 months with near-zero interview rates (HN threads), and the hiring freeze is hitting degree-holders. Meanwhile thousands of owner-run recycling businesses have no successor. Their storage and processing permits take years to obtain, and domestic scrap has just become strategic: the Aug 27, 2026 BIS rule forces black mass and tungsten scrap sellers to allocate 100% of sales to US buyers. Nobody packages this asset class for a first-time buyer.
solution: Build a target database from state solid-waste and hazardous-waste permit records, scrap-dealer licenses and owner age. Provide a standard diligence pack covering environmental liabilities and Phase I/II, fire history and insurance, permit transferability, commodity exposure and offtake contracts. Add a 90-day operator bootcamp with a mentor operator and introductions to SBA lenders. Take a fixed fee at close plus a small advisory equity stake.
why_now: AI-driven hiring freezes are producing a large pool of capable managers with cash and time. Greenfield battery and plastics recycling is capital-destroying (Ascend Elements and Li-Cycle bankruptcies, 7 of about 30 US PET reclaimers closed), while boring, permitted, cash-flowing yards look safer. DoD and DOE equity stakes and the BIS allocation rule are re-rating domestic scrap.
revenue_model: Cohort tuition (about $4-6K per seat). Buy-side success fee ($25-50K or 1.5-2% at close). 2-5% advisory equity in each acquisition. Sell-side listing fees from retiring owners. Diligence-pack licensing to lenders.
non_obvious_insight: In recycling the scarce input is not technology or capital but a competent successor operator, and the labor market is now manufacturing them. Permits are the moat, so the right move is to buy permitted cash flow instead of financing new plants.
first_30_days: Pull permit and owner-age lists for two states. Run a free webinar for laid-off managers through layoff-tracker and career communities and enroll a first cohort of about 10. Get two retiring owners to sign exclusive sell-side LOIs. Sign an environmental-consulting partner for a flat-fee diligence pack, and one SBA lender as the financing partner.

title: End-of-Life Pet Cell Banking via Aftercare Providers
one_liner: Sell a living-cell keepsake through pet crematories and euthanasia vets, and build a consented canine and feline cell-and-genome atlas for research.
customer: Grieving pet owners pay $249-399 per animal. Pet crematories, in-home euthanasia vets and cemeteries are distribution partners. Vet-pharma, AI-drug-discovery and academic groups license the consented, de-identified cell lines and genomes.
problem: Owners will pay for memorials, but the only 'living' option today is boutique cloning-linked gene banking at roughly $1,600+ that almost nobody hears about at the moment they need it. Aftercare providers touch millions of pets a year and have no biotech product. At the same time, AI-driven and vet drug discovery lack breed-annotated cell lines and genomes tied to full medical histories, and proprietary biological datasets are commanding large valuations (Basecamp raised $140M; Tempus is assembling 100k genomes).
solution: A low-cost collection kit (skin punch biopsy in transport medium, chilled shipping) handled by a vet or trained aftercare staff within 24-48 hours of death. A contract lab establishes and cryopreserves fibroblast lines for 20+ years, and optional whole-genome sequencing is included. Owners choose 'keep only' or a discounted 'keep and donate to research'. Consented lines plus medical-record metadata go into a research atlas that partners license.
why_now: High-profile celebrity pet cloning in late 2025 made living pet genetics a mainstream conversation. Whole-genome sequencing now costs roughly $100-200, and proprietary datasets are what AI-bio investors pay for. Pet aftercare is a large, emotionally trusted channel that no biotech has approached, and vet-shortage-driven consolidation is pushing clinics toward add-on revenue.
revenue_model: $249-399 per animal plus $60 per year storage. Partners earn $40-60 per kit. Research licensing of consented lines and genomes at $500-2,000 per line with metadata, plus dataset subscriptions. Unit costs are about $120-180 for culture and cryostorage.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource for pet biotech is not technology but trusted access to animals at the moment of death, and that access sits with crematories and euthanasia vets, not labs. Framing the purchase as optionality (cloning, future cell therapy) plus a donation option turns a grief moment into a data flywheel.
first_30_days: Contract an academic or commercial cell-banking lab for a validated tissue-to-line protocol. Sign 3-5 pet crematories or in-home euthanasia practices in one metro, and place 20 kits at a $99 introductory price. Recruit a supervising veterinarian and create an owner consent form covering research use. Take the first 30-50 lines to two vet-pharma or AI-biotech prospects for a data pilot.

title: Yield Twins and Robotic Cells for Regional Beef Packers
one_liner: Start with 3D vision yield scoring on the fabrication line and grow into robotic trimming cells for independent packers.
customer: Independent regional beef packers processing under about 2,000 head a day.
problem: Record cattle prices and a 75-year-low herd squeeze packer margins, while skilled knife labor is scarce and immigration enforcement hits meatpacking labor hardest.
solution: A camera-based yield-and-trim-loss scoring system for cut optimization, then robotic primal trimming and portioning cells sold as a service.
why_now: Physical-AI and 3D-vision costs dropped in 2025-26, and thin packer margins make a 1% yield gain worth millions.
revenue_model: Software at $2-4k per month per line first, then per-head fees for robotic cells.
non_obvious_insight: With margins this thin, the software yield gain pays before any robot works, and the data it collects trains the robot.
first_30_days: Visit three independent packers, mount cameras on a fab line, and deliver a first weekly yield report as a paid pilot.

title: Sponsor-a-Lifeline Satellite Messaging for Missionaries
one_liner: A church-sponsored satellite messaging line plus supporter-update relay for missionaries, Bible translators and mission-aviation crews in no-coverage areas, sold to mission agencies as duty of care.
customer: Mission agencies with 50-2,000 field workers and the sending churches that sponsor individual workers.
problem: Field workers live outside coverage and agencies carry duty of care using a patchwork of individual satellite communicators. Missionaries also fund themselves through supporter updates, which stall when connectivity is bad. Churches want a tangible way to care for their people, yet direct-to-cell carriers still do not know how to price or differentiate satellite service.
solution: A neutral bundle: direct-to-cell or handheld messaging across whichever networks work (Iridium NTN, Starlink direct-to-cell, others) plus an agency dashboard with check-in cadence, geofenced security alerts and evacuation triggers. Short satellite texts are compiled into a 'prayer letter' for supporters, and a sponsor page (for example 'Sponsor Anna's lifeline at $18 per month') keeps privacy controls.
why_now: Satellite-to-phone partnerships are multiplying but 'key questions remain unresolved' on pricing and value (Satellite Today, Sept 2026). Iridium NTN Direct is expected later in 2026, and Starlink ARPU falling from $81 to $66 signals cheaper plans. Carriers and resellers need verticals with a willing payer.
revenue_model: $15-25 per field worker per month paid by the agency or sponsors, a $150-200 hardware and setup margin, and enterprise duty-of-care dashboard tiers.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is the sending church or agency, not the traveler, and the value of connectivity is fundraising continuity as much as SOS. A 'sponsor a lifeline' framing turns safety hardware into recurring giving.
first_30_days: Approach 5 small and mid-sized agencies through a mission-agency association. Offer 20-seat pilots at $150 setup plus $18 per month per seat. Write prayer-letter templates and test the sponsor page with two sending churches.

title: Serial-Level Collateral Registry for GPU Lenders
one_liner: The independent field-exam firm and cross-lender double-pledge registry for AI hardware debt, built on the military rule that a serial number appears on one hand receipt only.
customer: Private-credit funds, banks, equipment lessors, ABS trustees and insurers financing neocloud GPU fleets, which now hold well over $20 billion in GPU-backed debt. Secondary: neoclouds that need audit-ready proof to borrow at lower spreads.
problem: Lenders rely on borrower-supplied serial lists, telemetry and occasional inspections. After the Tricolor and First Brands double-pledging scandals (the SEC charged Tricolor's former executives in August 2026), lenders know 'the same collateral pledged twice' is real. GPU servers sit in multi-tenant colocation halls, are easy to move, swap or re-pledge to another SPV, and telemetry can be spoofed. Serial-number UCC filings are rarely searched across lenders, and a colo technician paid by the borrower is not an independent counter.
solution: Three layers. (1) A repeatable two-person independent inventory protocol: witnessed reads of chassis label, BMC out-of-band serial and GPU-level serial, plus rack and cage photos, location and power draw. (2) Serialized tamper-evident seals on cages and rack doors, checked at each visit. (3) A privacy-preserving cross-lender registry of hashed serials so a lender learns whether a serial is already pledged elsewhere without revealing its book. Deliver monthly compliance packages that plug into the loan's reporting covenants for the trustee.
why_now: GPU-backed lending crossed $20 billion, and CoreWeave's $8.5 billion delayed-draw term loan (March 2026) showed the asset class reaching investment-grade structures. Tricolor and First Brands made 'verify the collateral independently' a board-level demand in private credit. Loan documents already grant lenders inspection rights, so the buyer has the access but not the in-house field-exam capability. Export-control diversion risk adds a second reason for chain-of-custody evidence.
revenue_model: Per-site audit of $15-50k, annual monitoring retainer of $50-250k per facility, registry subscriptions of $50-200k per lender, and trustee or insurer reporting packages. Long-term, per-basis-point fees on financed collateral under verification.
non_obvious_insight: Fraud lives at the seam between paper and physical, and the only reliable control is a count by someone who does not report to the borrower. That is what a military property book officer and a sensitive-item inventory do. Lenders will not share collateral lists with each other but will share hashes to avoid being second in line, so the registry becomes the moat. Telemetry proves a box is powered on, not that it is the box you financed.
first_30_days: Recruit 2-3 former property book or supply officers plus a data-center operations technician. Write and publish the audit protocol. Approach 5 mid-tier credit funds and equipment lenders (not the giants) that do GPU deals and lack field-exam staff. Offer a fixed-fee pilot audit on a live deal using the lender's existing inspection rights. Get a securities and privacy lawyer to bless the hashed-serial registry design before any lender data is pooled.

title: Help-Desk Reset Firewall for MSPs
one_liner: A plug-in for ConnectWise, Autotask and HaloPSA that makes it impossible for a technician to reset a password or MFA without out-of-band verification and manager approval.
customer: MSPs and outsourced IT help desks serving SMBs, priced per technician.
problem: IT help desks are a named target of voice deepfakes, and one report says over half of CISOs have seen a successful attack. An MSP technician is a single point of compromise for dozens of client tenants, and techs judge identity by voice and by facts attackers already have. SMB clients have no security team to catch it.
solution: A reset gate inside the ticket. MFA resets, password resets and new-device enrollments require verification through a contact and number pulled from the client's HR system or PSA (never from the caller), a manager approval push, a cooling-off delay with notification to the user's existing devices, and risk scoring (new country, odd hours). Evidence is stored for insurer questionnaires.
why_now: Help-desk social engineering drove major 2025 intrusions, voice cloning removes the tell, and insurers now ask about caller verification. Enterprise help-desk verification vendors ignore the MSP channel.
revenue_model: $15-30 per technician per month plus $1 per client user per month.
non_obvious_insight: MSPs are the most leveraged and least-served target. The control is a process lock, not a detector, so it does not decay when deepfakes improve, and insurance-renewal pressure makes it a required purchase.
first_30_days: Build it as a ConnectWise Manage/HaloPSA webhook plus a Teams approval bot. Recruit 10 MSPs from MSP peer groups and forums at $299 per month, and show the insurance-renewal benefit.

title: Exchange for Shelved Academic Projects and Null Data
one_liner: Buy the 'graveyard' of academic labs, meaning abandoned projects, validated knockout lines, half-built assays and failed-experiment data, and resell them as dossiers with an interview slot to seed biotechs and AI-bio data teams. Supply is anchored by a paid lab-closure clearance service.
customer: Sellers: departing postdocs, PIs downsizing or closing labs, and department chairs and EHS offices who must clear the space. Buyers: seed biotech founders, AI-bio and virtual-cell model companies that need experimental data including null results, pharma target-validation groups, and CROs that need validated cell models. Dossiers sell for $3-30k, and closure concierge fees run $5-15k.
problem: Every lab has a graveyard: KO lines, reporter constructs, a half-optimized assay, a screen that didn't pan out, and boxes in the -80 labeled 'JK 3/14 P3 #2'. When a postdoc leaves or a lab shrinks, the physical items are discarded or become orphaned, and the reasons the project failed leave in the postdoc's head. Meanwhile a startup or AI-bio team pays 12 months and $500k to rebuild the same tools and rediscover the same dead ends. Published literature is heavily biased toward positives, and models trained only on positives are systematically overconfident.
solution: Two-sided wedge. Supply side: 'Lab Closure Concierge' is a fixed-fee triage service for labs that are closing or downsizing. It inventories freezers, plasmids, cell lines and mouse lines, interviews the departing postdoc for 90 minutes to capture provenance and failure reasons (transcribed and structured with AI), disposes of hazardous items compliantly, and flags what is worth keeping. Demand side: a curated catalog of 'dossiers': the physical or digital assets, protocols, raw data including nulls, plus a paid call with the person who built them. Use a standard institutional license or MTA template with a revenue share to the university, so overloaded tech-transfer offices approve it because the alternative is a dumpster.
why_now: NIH grant terminations, indirect-cost fights and uncertain 2026 budgets are pushing labs to shrink or close. Biotech shutdowns have also left surplus bench assets (verify current scale). AI-bio companies are openly short of high-quality experimental data, especially negative data, and pay for it. Tech-transfer offices are understaffed. LLM transcription and structuring turns a 90-minute interview into a searchable dossier cheaply.
revenue_model: Closure-concierge flat fee paid by the department or PI. A 25-30% commission on dossier sales, with revenue share to seller and institution. Annual data-subscription tier for AI-bio buyers (curated null-result feeds).
non_obvious_insight: The vials are worth very little. The value is provenance plus the 'why it failed' story stored in one person's memory, and it evaporates the day the postdoc's visa or contract ends. So the product is not a marketplace for samples, it is structured exit-knowledge capture with a physical-asset appendix. Because the university owns the IP anyway, the clean structure is to make the institution a paid party rather than an obstacle.
first_30_days: Use your own postdoc network to line up 3-5 labs that are shrinking or have departing postdocs. Offer a free triage-and-catalog audit in exchange for permission to list a few assets. Produce 10 dossiers with structured interviews. Cold-email 30 seed biotechs and AI-bio data leads with the top 5 dossiers. Close one sale at $3-8k. Use that transaction to test the university revenue-share template with one tech-transfer office.

title: Neighborhood Block Wildfire Cover via HOAs
one_liner: Softer reinsurance isn't reaching homeowners, so aggregate a mitigated neighborhood into one certified risk that capital will price like a portfolio instead of 300 anonymous parcels.
customer: HOA boards and Firewise-style communities of 200-2,000 homes in wildfire states (CA, CO, UT, NM, OR) where members are being nonrenewed or pushed to FAIR plans.
problem: Nonrenewals are at records and carriers price parcel by parcel, ignoring community-level mitigation like hydrants, vegetation control, ember vents and evacuation routes. Reinsurance is softening (Jefferies expects declines through 2027) but primary policyholders see none of it.
solution: Community risk certification, drone-verified and re-certified annually, plus block placement with an MGA or coverholder writing group-rated homeowner policies backed by reinsurance or ILS capital. The HOA collects dues, funds a shared deductible reserve and enforces mitigation standards.
why_now: California passed three claims and nonrenewal bills on 2026-09-03. Cat bond issuance is a record $18.9B year to date. Softening means capital is abundant and looking for well-defined books, and nonrenewals are a midterm political flashpoint.
revenue_model: MGA commission of about 12-15% of premium, $40-$100 per home for certification, and an HOA subscription for compliance tracking.
non_obvious_insight: In a soft market capital is abundant, and what's scarce is a verifiable, homogeneous risk pool. An HOA is a ready-made legal aggregator with dues collection and enforcement powers, which solves distribution and adverse selection together.
first_30_days: Approach 20 HOA management companies and Firewise sites in California foothills and Colorado's Front Range. Offer a free community risk-certification report. Sign one pilot LOI and line up an MGA willing to quote a block program.

title: Lifeboat for Students of Closing Colleges
one_liner: A transfer-rescue service that maps every credit of a closing college's students into a receiving school's degree requirements, paid flat-fee by institutions and states, free to students.
customer: Payers: closing or distressed private colleges (which must file teach-out plans), state higher-ed agencies and accreditors, and regional receiving colleges that want transfer enrollment. Users: students at the closing school, roughly 500 to 3,000 per small college.
problem: When a small college closes, teach-out deals are improvised. Nursing, education and arts credits often fail to map. Students face a murky choice, because entering a teach-out forfeits closed-school loan discharge. Transcripts become hard to get, and many students simply stop out. One tally counts nine college closures in 2026, and Philadelphia Fed modeling points to dozens more.
solution: Within a week of an announced closure, ingest the catalog, syllabi and transcripts into a credit-mapping engine and produce course-by-course equivalency offers from 3 to 5 receiving schools. Give each student a lifeboat file: credits accepted, remaining requirements, time to degree, net price, and the teach-out versus transfer versus loan-discharge tradeoff, in plain language. Add written articulation letters from receiving schools, warm handoffs to admissions, and transcript custody. Offer a paid advocacy tier for credit-denial appeals.
why_now: The US high-school graduating class peaked in 2025 (about 3.9M) and shrinks about 13% by 2041, so the tuition-dependent-college shakeout is just starting. LLMs can now match syllabi to course equivalencies in hours, work that used to take registrars weeks per student. Receiving schools are hungry for transfer enrollment and closing schools have no bandwidth.
revenue_model: Flat fees only: a closure-response engagement ($25k to $75k) paid by the closing school, its state agency or a consortium; an annual credit-mapping and closure-readiness subscription ($30k to $100k) from receiving colleges; and a $149 to $299 student advocacy add-on. Do not charge per enrolled student, because the Higher Education Act's incentive-compensation ban prohibits enrollment bounties at Title IV schools (confirm with counsel).
non_obvious_insight: Students at a closing college are the highest-intent, highest-credit leads in higher education, but the bounty model that would normally monetize them is illegal, so the business must be paid for labor and neutrality instead. The moat is a growing corpus of verified course equivalencies plus being the trusted neutral on day one of a closure. Accreditors and state agencies need a vendor for teach-out compliance and do not want to be seen picking winners among rival colleges.
first_30_days: Build a tracker of announced and at-risk closures from accreditor notices and news. Pick the two nearest announced closures and offer their registrars and the state higher-ed agency a free pilot for one program (nursing or education). Line up 3 nearby receiving colleges' transfer directors. Hand-run LLM-assisted credit mapping on 50 students with a contract registrar reviewing, and deliver personal lifeboat files. Close the first flat-fee pilot with a receiving college or state agency, and publish a 'What to do when your college closes' guide for inbound.

title: Design-for-Duty: Engineer Below the 15% Metal Line
one_liner: A CAD/BOM tool that redesigns imported products to fall under Section 232's metal-weight cliffs or qualify for the 10% US-melt rate.
customer: Product-engineering and sourcing leads at $20M-$500M brands that import metal-heavy goods (furniture, fitness gear, grills, hand tools, lighting, enclosures, HVAC accessories).
problem: Since 2026-04-06 metals duties apply to full customs value: 50% on primary metal, 25% on derivatives, and 10% if made with US-melted steel or US-smelted aluminum/copper. Products under 15% metal weight are excluded (per Foley; verify current text). More derivative articles were proposed on 2026-08-06. Insiders treat this as a sourcing or lobbying problem. Brokers and freight forwarders cannot change a bill of materials, and engineers do not know the cliff exists.
solution: A plugin and standalone tool that ingests CAD mass properties and the BOM (SolidWorks, Fusion, Onshape or CSV). It computes metal weight share per SKU and simulates variants, such as a polymer or wood part in place of a steel bracket, or one US-melted component. It returns duty-weighted landed cost per variant and drafts the engineering change order. It also flags SKUs sitting just above a tier boundary.
why_now: The IEEPA tariffs fell on 2026-02-20 and the regime moved onto Section 232. Metal content is now the biggest variable in landed cost. Full-value duties began in April 2026, and the August 2026 proposal adds derivative products.
revenue_model: SaaS at $1.5-4k a month per product line. Launch-phase audits at $1.5k per SKU. Optional 10-15% share of first-year duty saved on redesigned SKUs.
non_obvious_insight: The tariff is a bill-of-materials problem, not a country problem. A few points of mass shifted can be worth more than moving a factory, and no one in the chain (broker, freight forwarder, sourcing agent) is paid to touch the design.
first_30_days: Pull public bill-of-lading data for HTS chapters exposed to metal derivatives. Cold-email 100 product heads offering a free one-SKU cliff check. Sell 10 fixed-price SKU audits at $1.5k, done in a spreadsheet. Retain a customs attorney to confirm how metal weight is measured. Build the plugin once patterns repeat.

title: Supervised-Hours Bench for Counselors and Social Workers
one_liner: A managed group-supervision network and hour-logging platform that lets clinics fund the thousands of post-degree supervised hours gating counseling, MFT and social-work licenses.
customer: Group therapy practices, community mental-health agencies and school districts hiring associate-level counselors and social workers; the associates themselves.
problem: Counseling, psychology and social work were excluded from the higher federal loan cap. Licensure typically requires 2-4k supervised hours after the degree, and associates often pay $50-150 an hour out of pocket for supervision that is scarce and tracked on paper. Clinics cannot hire associates faster than supervisors can be found.
solution: Certified supervisors, often semi-retired licensed clinicians, deliver state-compliant group supervision by video. The platform logs hours in board-ready format and enforces state ratios and rules. Clinics pay per associate per month to onboard associates who can bill insurance under supervision.
why_now: The July 2026 loan caps squeeze students in excluded fields and push them toward employer support. Behavioral-health demand is high, and telesupervision is widely permitted in many states after the pandemic.
revenue_model: $150-300 per associate per month from the clinic, supervision delivery margin, and hour-logging SaaS. Optional share of billed associate revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input in the credential chain is not the degree but post-degree supervision, and the payer is the employer, not the student, because associates bill insurance and become revenue-positive once supervised.
first_30_days: Pick one large state that permits telesupervision. Recruit 5 licensed supervisors. Sign 3 group practices with about 10 associates in total. Run the hour logs in spreadsheets first and charge $200 per associate per month. Verify board rules before selling.

title: First-72-Hours Concierge for Paid Communities
one_liner: An outcome-priced service that staffs experienced ex-power-mods to personally handle every new member's first three days in creator-run paid communities, cutting the week-one churn that drains recurring revenue.
customer: Owners of paid communities with 500-20,000 paying members on Skool, Circle, Discord, Mighty Networks or Patreon: course creators and trading, fitness and business coaches doing $50k-$1M+ per month.
problem: Skool operator guides say about 60% of churners decide in week one, and average monthly churn sits around 12-18%. Owners cover the front door with random volunteers or VAs posting templated welcomes. New members' first posts go unanswered for a day. Scam DMs from fake admins ('send USDT to verify') hit newcomers hardest. The first unexplained removal or cold reply turns a paying member into a refund request.
solution: Small pods of trained ex-moderators run the first 72 hours: a personal welcome, a reply to every first post within 2 hours across time zones, routing to the right thread, removal of impersonators and scam DMs, and gentle handling of first-time rule breaks so the person stays. AI drafts and triages, but a human always sends. Each community gets a rules-as-code playbook and a weekly cohort-retention report with a holdout group so the effect is measurable. Work stays on Discord, Skool and Circle, so it doesn't collide with Reddit's Rule 5.
why_now: Reddit began enforcing its five-community moderator cap on 31 March 2026. That has pushed many experienced volunteer mods into Advisor/Alumni roles and left them open to paid work on platforms the cap doesn't cover. Creator-run paid communities have grown into real revenue businesses, while AI slop and scam DMs make the new-member experience worse.
revenue_model: A base fee of $1.5k-$4k per month per community plus an outcome kicker of 10-20% of retained MRR uplift versus a holdout. Mods are paid $15-$25 per hour, giving roughly 40-50% gross margin.
non_obvious_insight: In big subreddits a newcomer whose first comment is removed without explanation almost never returns. Retention is decided in the first three days by one human interaction, not by content quality. That makes moderation a retention function, not a cost center, so it should be priced by churn saved, not hours worked. It is also hard to outsource to a generic trust-and-safety BPO, because tone and judgment are the product.
first_30_days: Recruit 10-15 ex-power-mods from mod Discords and r/ModSupport who lost seats under the cap. Write a one-page playbook. Approach 30 owners of Skool communities with 1k+ paying members, using the public discovery listings. Offer a $750, 14-day pilot in which half of new joiners get the concierge and half don't. Report the day-14 retention delta and convert the best results into monthly contracts.

title: Clinic-Sponsored Tuition for Loan-Capped PT Students
one_liner: Sports-medicine PT and athletic-training employers fund tuition for students shut out of federal loans, in return for a structured work commitment.
customer: Multi-site outpatient orthopedic and sports PT groups, performance-rehab clinics and athletic-training staffing contractors pay the fee. The beneficiaries are DPT and athletic-training students facing the new loan caps.
problem: Since July 1, 2026, grad loans are capped at $20.5k a year and $100k total, and PT, OT, nursing and counseling were left out of the 'professional' tier ($50k a year, $200k total). A $100-150k DPT can no longer be financed federally. Private lenders are tightening, some loans reach 16% APR, and disbursements ran up to 6 weeks late. Meanwhile clinics have chronic PT vacancies and pay recruiters roughly 15-25% of first-year salary per hire.
solution: A sponsored-seat platform. The clinic pledges tuition support paid directly to the school, using tax-free employer educational assistance (up to $5,250 a year under Section 127) plus scholarship funds. The student signs a transparent 3-year post-licensure commitment with pro-rated forgiveness, structured around state limits on stay-or-pay clauses. We handle matching, contracts, compliance and servicing. Any remaining gap routes to a CDFI or credit-union partner that underwrites on the employer's offer.
why_now: The caps went live with the fall 2026 semester, so the first affected cohorts are hitting the gap now. A healthcare-association lawsuit (suspension deadline December 2026) adds uncertainty, so students and programs want a hedge whichever way it goes. Recruiting costs are high, and the tax-free employer student-loan-repayment exclusion was made permanent in 2025.
revenue_model: A success fee of 8-12% of first-year salary (about $9-13k per seat), below the recruiter benchmark: one third at contract signing, the rest at licensure start. Plus a servicing fee of 0.5-1% on managed balances and a referral fee from the partner lender.
non_obvious_insight: Federal caps have made employers the only underwriter that can price DPT risk, because salary, licensure pass rates and vacancy cost are all known. For a clinic group, tuition-for-service is a cheaper and stickier recruiting channel than a 20% recruiter fee. It also locks in local talent in the years when the pipeline shrinks.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 PT-group owners through APTA state chapters and practice-owner communities. Sign 10 sponsored seats for the Jan/Aug 2027 cohorts. Ask 3-4 DPT programs' financial-aid offices to introduce enrolled students with funding gaps. Use a counsel-drafted contract template. No lending is needed at first; the launch product is a paid placement plus a contract.

title: Operator-of-Record for Enterprise Drone Flights
one_liner: A licensed BVLOS operations team-as-a-service that files the waivers, runs the safety case and supervises the flights for utilities, solar developers and pipeline owners.
customer: Mid-size utilities and co-ops, solar and wind developers, pipeline and rail operators, ports, mines, and their insurers.
problem: BVLOS technology is ready, but organizations lack the capability: waiver applications, safety cases, ops manuals, remote-pilot staffing and data pipelines. The final status of Part 108 (the FAA BVLOS rule) could not be verified, which adds uncertainty. Meanwhile the DJI ban forces fleet refreshes.
solution: A reusable safety-case library and remote-pilot center (one pilot supervising 5-10 drone docks) running US-made drone-in-a-box fleets. Price per line-mile or per site, with data delivered into the customer's GIS and maintenance systems.
why_now: The December 2025 DJI restrictions force fleet replacement decisions in 2026, and Wing's 1M deliveries show BVLOS operations working at scale. Whatever Part 108's final form, operators still need documented safety cases and waivers.
revenue_model: $5-20k per month per site retainer or per-line-mile pricing on multi-year MSAs, plus waiver and safety-case consulting fees.
non_obvious_insight: Regulation is a one-time cost that vendors avoid, but the operator-of-record that accumulates waivers, flight logs and accepted safety cases builds a moat that compounds with every approval.
first_30_days: Pick one region (for example co-ops in Texas or Colorado) and partner with one US-made dock vendor. Get one co-op to sign a pilot covering 20 substations, file the waiver, and aim for the first inspection within 60 days.

title: Front Door for AI Callers at Local Businesses
one_liner: A phone-number layer that recognizes when the caller is an AI agent, answers instantly with pre-authorized quotes and availability, and routes real customers to humans.
customer: Owner-operated local service businesses (salons, groomers, HVAC and plumbing, auto shops, cleaners) with 1-20 staff, reached via marketing agencies and booking or field-service platforms. AI receptionist vendors are later licensees.
problem: Google's 'Have AI check pricing' agentic calling has rolled out to US Search users and expanded to home services in summer 2026. Businesses now get AI callers that tie up staff and harvest prices, and owners cannot tell agents from customers. In Microsoft's Magentic Marketplace simulation, buyer agents heavily favored the first proposal they received, so fast structured answers win business.
solution: Answer with an agent detector and an agent lane. If the caller identifies as or behaves like an AI (or presents a signed handshake), reply with a spoken and machine-readable quote from the owner's rate card and calendar within owner-set bounds, and log the outcome. Real customers go to humans. Publish a URL or DTMF handshake so compliant agents can switch from speech to structured data, the Gibberlink idea done with production-grade channels. Analytics show which agents call and quote win rates.
why_now: Agentic calling is live at Google scale, AI receptionists are common, and the 2025 Gibberlink demo proved the handshake idea but remains a proof of concept. Production agent protocols (MCP, A2A) do not cover phone calls to small businesses.
revenue_model: $49-$149/month per location, agency white-label deals, and later per-verified-handshake fees from agent platforms.
non_obvious_insight: The phone is the API of the local economy and both ends are becoming machines that still talk in speech. Whoever owns the switch-to-data handshake and the seller's rate-card truth owns local agent commerce, and speed to first quote may matter more than price.
first_30_days: Build the call flow on a telephony API. Recruit 20 salons, groomers and HVAC shops through 3 local marketing agencies, log the AI calls they receive (many owners are unaware), and show AI calls answered and quotes won. Charge $79/month.

title: Side-Selling Early Warning for Milk and Coffee Coops
one_liner: A churn-prediction and targeted-advance service that tells dairy and coffee cooperatives which farmers are about to side-sell to cash brokers, and triggers the right cash intervention before the volume walks away.
customer: Managers and boards of medium-sized dairy cooperatives (about 2,000-10,000 farmers), coffee cooperative societies and factories, and mid-sized processors that buy from farmer groups. They pay because lost throughput hits fixed factory costs and credit recovery.
problem: Side-selling is the silent killer of Kenyan coops. Farmers sell milk to hawkers and raw-milk traders, or coffee cherry to cash buyers, who pay on the spot, while the coop pays monthly or later and then deducts for feeds, inputs, AI services and loans. Deliveries fade slowly, not suddenly, so managers notice too late. Side-selling spikes when a farmer's net pay is squeezed by deductions, when payment is late, or in cash-crunch weeks such as January and other school fee dates, funerals and sickness. Coops respond with lectures and warnings instead of predicting and fixing the cash gap.
solution: Ingest the coop's delivery and payment history (usually already exported from the weighing or dairy management software). A simple gradient-boosted or rule-based model scores each farmer weekly for side-selling risk using delivery drift, missed pay days, deductions as a share of gross, days since last payment, seasonality and school-term calendars. The coop gets a daily short list for its field officer, with SMS or voice-call scripts in the local language. The intervention is a coop-funded, capped advance or deduction holiday for at-risk farmers in their predicted cash-crunch window, since the coop already holds the delivered stock and the farmer's record as collateral. It measures recovered litres or kilos against a control group.
why_now: Global arabica prices spiked to record highs in 2025 and pulled cherry towards cash brokers in Kenya, at the same time as coffee-sector reforms push coops to pay faster and more transparently. Weighing scales and dairy management software have digitised delivery data at many coops over the last five years, so the data now exists. M-Pesa bulk disbursement makes weekly or on-demand advances cheap. Modern ML tooling makes a credible model a two-week job rather than a research project. I could not verify current legal specifics, so confirm the latest coffee and dairy regulations and data-protection obligations (coop as data controller) before pilots.
revenue_model: Performance fee of roughly 5-10% of recovered volume value (paid from the additional milk or cherry that stays in the coop), or a SaaS retainer of a few tens of thousands of shillings per month per coop. Later, licensing the model to processors and lenders who want a farmer reliability signal.
non_obvious_insight: Side-selling is not disloyalty, it is a rational response to cash-flow timing. The winning intervention is not a scolding letter but a small advance placed at the right moment, funded by the coop's own working capital. It is also predictable from delivery patterns weeks before it happens, because farmers taper deliveries before they stop. Most agritech sells farmers new products, whereas here the buyer is the institution that quietly loses 10% or more of its volume.
first_30_days: Get 24 months of delivery and payment CSVs from one or two coops, ideally through your own parents' society or the manager you know personally. Build the risk model in a notebook, deliver a top-200 at-risk list plus a script, and run a 60-day test where half the list gets the SMS and advance offer and half does not. Agree to be paid only on retained volume compared to the control group, and use the result as the case study for the next five coops.

title: Certified Refurb Phone Pipeline for Africa
one_liner: The memory crunch kills the cheap new phone, so the next wave of African users arrives on graded, warrantied used handsets.
customer: Independent phone retailers and mid-size distributors in Nigeria, Kenya and Ghana, and telco handset-financing programmes.
problem: Memory is 30-40% of a phone's bill of materials, IDC calls sub-Rs 9,000 phones possibly permanently uneconomical, and the GSMA $40 phone is only a pilot. About 960M Africans under coverage are still offline, and the used-phone market is full of blacklisted, dying-battery lemons.
solution: Buy bulk trade-in lots from the Gulf, EU and Japan and grade them in software (battery health, IMEI/blacklist check, Play certification). Ship with a 6-month warranty and sell to retailers on 30-day credit. The wedge is IMEI-clean, warrantied lots for a handful of retailers in one market such as Lagos.
why_now: 2026 AI-driven memory prices broke the sub-$60 new-phone tier, and LatAm shipments fell 10%. The GSMA is piloting a $40 phone precisely because the market cannot produce one.
revenue_model: Roughly $8-15 gross margin per handset, plus warranty fees and a financing spread.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders wait for cheap new phones. The scarce asset is trust in used devices, and whoever certifies them owns the affordable tier once new supply disappears.
first_30_days: Source about 500 units from a Dubai or European refurbisher, grade them and place them with five retailers on consignment. Track return rates, which become the pricing moat.

title: Vacant-Unit Meter Watchdog and Insurance Vacancy Log
one_liner: Uses utility smart-meter data that owners already have rights to, so PMs can catch squatters, leaks and freeze risk in empty units within hours, without installing any hardware.
customer: Property managers and owners of single-family and 2-to-20-unit portfolios (100 to 2,000 doors). They already pay the utilities on vacant units and carry standard dwelling or small-building policies with a vacancy clause. Buyer is the PM's ops director or the owner. Secondary buyers later are E&S and landlord-program insurers.
problem: When a unit is occupied, the tenant is the sensor and tells you about leaks. When it is vacant you are blind for 20 to 60 days. Water damage, squatters, stolen copper, AC left running and burst pipes all happen in that window. Most property policies restrict vandalism, water damage and theft after roughly 60 days of vacancy, and the claim gets denied or cut exactly when the loss is biggest. Squatter removal is also time-critical: in many states an intruder found on day 2 is a police trespass matter, while the same person on day 30 needs a months-long court eviction. Walk-throughs are weekly at best, and the maintenance tech skips them when busy.
solution: Vacancy Vitals connects to interval electric and water data through owner-authorized utility APIs (Green Button Connect, or aggregators like UtilityAPI). The owner's account is usually the one active during vacancy, so no tenant consent is needed. Rules fire on patterns: continuous 24/7 water flow (leak), electric baseline above the empty-unit norm (someone living there, a crypto miner, a grow), a heating or cooling setpoint far outside range (pipe-freeze or mold risk), and a sudden drop to zero in a unit that should be running HVAC. Alerts go by text to the on-call tech with a one-tap 'send someone' button. The product also generates a time-stamped weekly vacancy-inspection log (data check plus a tech photo check-in) formatted for carriers' vacancy-permit or inspection conditions. That log is what preserves coverage.
why_now: Anti-squatter laws were passed in a wave in 2024 and 2025 (for example Florida and Georgia), which makes early detection more valuable. Smart-meter penetration passed roughly 70% of US electric customers. Insurers have been tightening on water-damage and vacancy exposure for several years. AI-based anomaly detection on interval data is now cheap. (Current state-by-state anti-squatter rules and utility API coverage should be verified before launch.)
revenue_model: $4 to $7 per vacant-unit-month on usage, or a flat $1 to $2 per door per month portfolio subscription. Later, insurer-paid or insurer-discounted programs: the carrier pays a fee per monitored door in exchange for lower loss ratios and a vacancy-clause waiver.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest sensor for a vacant house is the meter the utility already installed, and the account is in the owner's name during vacancy. Nobody in proptech treats owner-account utility data as a security and insurance-compliance feed. They sell $60 leak sensors and cameras instead. The other secret is legal timing. The value is not detecting the squatter, it is detecting them in the first 48 hours, when the law treats it as trespass rather than a tenancy.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 to 5 SFR or small-multifamily PMs, offer a free 'backtest', and pull 12 months of interval data for units that were vacant. Show them the incidents the tool would have caught. These are usually a few leaks, a few unauthorized occupants and several HVAC-left-on units, each worth $1,000 to $15,000. Build a UtilityAPI-based prototype with three rules, text alerts and a weekly PDF log. Charge $99 per month per portfolio during the pilot, then convert to per-unit pricing. In parallel, talk to two independent insurance agents who write landlord programs, to learn the exact vacancy-permit language and to get a warm intro for the carrier channel.

title: Pharmacy Friendly Calls, Paid by Adherence Stars
one_liner: Independent pharmacies run weekly human-led friendship calls to isolated refill customers, funded by the Medicare adherence performance that loneliness quietly erodes.
customer: Independent community pharmacies (roughly 18,000 in the US) paying $500-1,200 a month per store, later reimbursed through Medicare Advantage and Part D plan performance and MTM contracts.
problem: Isolated older adults skip refills. Adherence measures for diabetes, RAS-antagonist and statin drugs carry triple weight in Medicare Star ratings, so plans pay for every point. Older adults distrust AI companions (Pew, Jun 2026: 40-46% of 65+ are 'unsure' whether chatbots help or hurt), and startup elder-companion services lack a trusted local face. The corner pharmacist has that trust and a list of exactly who is isolated.
solution: A 'Pharmacy Pal' program. Each store enrolls 40-80 living-alone or homebound refill customers. A paid part-time caller (a retiree or pharmacy tech) makes a weekly 10-minute call using an AI-prepared brief (last call notes, refill gaps, birthdays), and also does a twice-monthly delivery run. Software covers rosters, call briefs, refill-gap alerts and a proportion-of-days-covered dashboard the pharmacy can show plans. The AI never talks to the patient.
why_now: Chain-store closures (Rite Aid's 2025 wind-down among them) made independents the last local pharmacy for many seniors. Plans are squeezed on Star bonuses and margins and want cheap, measurable adherence levers. Pew's 2026 data show older adults distrust chatbots, which reopens the case for human-led programs.
revenue_model: $12-18 per enrolled patient per month, paid by the pharmacy out of retained refills, delivery fees and plan MTM or performance-network payments. Phase two is direct plan contracts priced on measured adherence lift.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders look for an elder-companion buyer among families and social-service agencies. The real loneliness budget for older adults sits inside Star-rating adherence economics, and the trusted delivery channel is the local pharmacist, not an app.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 independent pharmacies through state pharmacist associations and PSAO newsletters. Each pulls 40 patients from refill-gap reports. Run the calls manually with a spreadsheet and an LLM-generated brief. Measure adherence lift against matched non-enrolled patients over 90 days. Charge $500 a month per store from the start.
